entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The Soap Creek Valley History Project was initially authorized in 1989 by Dr. William Atkinson, former Director of the OSU Research Forests. The oral history portion of this project remained under Dr. Atkinson's direction until January 1994, when it was assigned to Jeffrey Garver, OSU Research Forests Manager. In December of that year responsibility for the oral histories was given to Ann Rogers, Cultural Resources Manager for OSU Research Forests. Funding for the Soap Creek Valley History Project is provided by the OSU College of Forestry.

entries.speaker: editorial

Holly Behm Losli, Tami Torres and Md. Shahidul Islam, OSU Research Forests text editors, completed final formatting and indexing under the direction of Pam Beebee, OSU Research Forests Office Manager. This project could not have been completed without the help of these people.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: THE SOAP CREEK VALLEY HISTORY PROJECT

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The Soap Creek Valley History Project was undertaken by the Oregon State University's Research Forests in 1989 for the purpose of better understanding the history, ecology, and culture of an area that has been impacted by OSU land management practices for nearly seventy years. An important part of the project has been the location and publications of existing recorded oral history interviews with individuals who have had an influence upon the valley's history. New recordings have also been made with significant individuals who have not been previously consulted, as well as "follow-up" interviews with a few people who have continued to contribute to our understanding of the Soap Creek area.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The publication of these interviews as a series of cross-referenced and indexed monographs has been undertaken in an effort to make them available to resource managers, researchers and educators. An additional use is accurate and accessible references for a planned written history of the area.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: One of the primary accomplishments of the Soap Creek Valley History Project has been the creation of a computerized concordance file, currently in IBM Word Perfect 5.1. This was made possible through the assistance and expertise of Bonnie Humphrey, of the former Horner Museum staff, Lisa Buschman, former secretary for the OSU Research Forests, and Holly Behm Losli and Tami Torres, text editor for OSU Research Forests. In 1994, the concordance file was thoroughly tested and redesigned under the direction of Md. Shahidul Islam, currently the publications editor of this project. His refinement of the concordance file now allows for a more efficient and systematic indexing of the monographs in this series. In addition, the system will now be much easier for students, staff and others to use, and will provide a better method for cross-referencing other research materials being used in the construction of a scholarly history of this project

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The Soap Creek Valley history is being assembled from the written and spoken words of the people who made it and lived it. The use of the concordance file allows information from the journal entries of botanist David Douglas, the transcribed words of Kalapuyan William Hartless, the spoken memories of pioneer "Grandma" Carter, and the recordings of Charles and Norman Hindes to be systematically searched and organized. The index to this monograph is an example of the applied use of the file.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: INTRODUCTION

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Charles and Norman Hindes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We came to Soap Creek from the McCoy-Burtrom logging and sawmill operation in Kings Valley, Oregon in 1928, just in time to enroll in Tampico School for the 1928-29 school year. Soap Creek school was not in operation at that time. During the summer months, before the economic crash of 1929, and on Saturdays, we carried drinking water to the cutting crew and greased the crossties on the skid road for the horse loggers. With the stock market crash came an almost over night closure of all logging and milling operations. We had no income, no government assistance in any form, and all the young people with new 1928 Model A Fords purchased on credit had them repossessed. The remaining three years (1930-1932) were the most severe of the Depression Years. There are few photographs from this time because people generally couldn't afford to buy cameras or film

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: An accidental encounter with Bob Zybach led to the writing of this oral history. My brother Norman and I, working with Bob and his associates, have endeavored to fill in a blank in Soap Creek Valley history -- and specifically, a two-year period in Soap Creek School chronology -- that had not been previously documented.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We dedicate our efforts to as many named individuals as we can remember, and to any un-named residents residing in the McCoy/Burtrom saw mill site in the years 1928-31, and the heirs thereof. We have also mentioned some of the long time residents of the Valley with whom we had contact. When asked by Bob for photographs covering this period of time, neither Norman nor I could remember the family ever having anything by way of a box camera. And definitely after the mill closed, film and the developing thereof was a luxury we could not afford.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Although our time at mill/logging camp site was relatively short, it had a pronounced effect on we three boys. Our step-brother, Douglas Gilliam, while not included in the Soap Creek interview, was part of the family and of many of our activities during our stay in Soap Creek Valley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Prior to the stock market crash and start of "The Depression," which culminated in the closing of the mill, we boys had profound learning experiences. When not in school we had numerous household chores, such as carrying water (1/4 mile up hill), cutting winter firewood, etc. We also had some chores related to the logging and mill operation, such as cleaning out the horse barn (six horses deposit a substantial amount of used hay). One job I remember well was carrying water to the timber cutters. As I brought the empty water sacks down to be filled I would bring a bucket of grease and place a dab of grease on every skid (approximately 8' apart) on the skid road to enable the logs to slide with less resistance for the horses. Naturally, inasmuch as I was going up and down the hill at least twice a day, anything the "cutters" needed, such as a new axe or saw, file, or wedge, was added to my uphill trek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We three boys developed a good work ethic as well as an affinity for the logging industry. In addition, we learned many things by observing what to do and what not to do if one intended to be a long-lived logger. The seed was well planted for between the three of us we account for in excess of 75 year logging, milling and log hauling experience without major mishap.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When we first arrived in camp, Tampico was the nearest school, so for most of the first year we walked the 3.8 miles each way. After a time, Alvie Govier and his Model T truck with a wooden box built over a bare chassis were brought into serve as a school bus. It was rustic but superior to that 7.6 mile walk rain or shine.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For our last two years at the mill site a farm house was secured and Ms. Lottie Blake brought in to teach at what I am lead to believe was the second location of Soap Creek school. The house had been the Modrell home located roughly half way between the McCoy farm home and that of Elmer Govier on the west side of Soap Creek road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When Mrs. Blake entered our lives it denoted a turning point in all our lives, and mine in particular. Her strong point was history , but high school and college education were also high on her list of things to achieve in life. I learned many things from Mrs. Blake (not taught in higher education) of what to do and what not to do for success in education.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Earlier I mentioned we dedicated our efforts in this publication to as many individuals and families as we could remember that lived in the camp between the year 1928-31. I wish to modify that statement to read any one still living, after all 1996 is many years after the fact.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The following interview was conducted by Bob Zybach with Charles and Norman Hindes at 530 NW 15th, Corvallis, Oregon on September 28, 1993. Norman, Charles and Bob are looking at maps of Valley Mills before 1929.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1. Family History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'd like to start first by talking about your family history and maybe going back to your grandparents or your great grandparents on either your mother or father's side and bringing them forward in time to figure out why you got to Soap Creek in the first place.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well, granddad, grandmother came out here (to Oregon) in early 1900. . . They settled near Brownsville out there in the rain and bought that wheat ranch.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] More nearly Halsey.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Halsey, yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] They originated from a farm near Rockford, Illinois. I think they came out just shortly after the Lewis and Clark exposition in Portland around 1905 to 1907.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] And then we settled there on this big ranch and from there on, Chuck, you'll have to carry it on from there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do, do you remember you're grandfather's, name? In, Illinois?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yes, I do, in fact I was showing Norman some things this morning where my grandfather, my paternal grandfather and maternal grandfather were involved in an oil well exploration near the LaComb area and I have the stock certificate with both of their names on it which predates my mother and father's marriage. Now I don't know whether their joint business venture had any bearing on mother and father getting together but it was dated in 1913 and it was about 1915 before my mother and father were married. But going back to my father's early history; he originated in Wisconsin and in fact, his mother, my grandmother, came from near Madison, Wisconsin. But, after marrying grandfather Hindes, they farmed near Rockford, Illinois. While I was in the service during World War II, I endeavored to look up some of the family in Illinois but was only able to find a couple of business ventures in the Hindes name. One, a florist business and I don't remember what the other one was in and near Rockford. But there was quite a large family, possibly six or seven brothers on my grandfather's side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then did his wife have children from her previous marriage?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I don't think so. I don't think there were any other children involved. I'm in the process of doing some genealogical work but I haven't gotten back that far on grandmother Hindes' side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, do you know anything about her family, her maiden name or where she came from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No, I don't. My recollection is that she had the name of Johnson. Now, whether that was her married name or maiden name, I couldn't say. I'm in the process of doing some work on that. In fact, my youngest son is assisting with some

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: computerized information. To this point it has been primarily on my mother's side. And, this involved the Wood family who originated in Maine. Do you want to say anything about them, Norman?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Go ahead. You go ahead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, I don't want to dominate the conversation. Anytime you want to add something please do. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No, no. Go ahead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] ... We havea pretty fair documentation, from two aunts. One of them is 84, 85 now and she has documented most of this for Norman and I. Until this came along, we didn't have much contact with my mother's people. My mother died during the flu epidemic of 1919! when I was four months old and, of course, my father remarried and most of the family on my mother's side gravitated back to the east coast again, settling primarily in Florida.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did your mom die during the flu epidemic?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In Albany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, in Albany, Oregon. So, that was right here in Oregon.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Right.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] 1919, yeah. Flu.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And, so, really we didn't have any contact at all with my mother's family until after we had moved to Tillamook and Norman went to . . . What hospital was it?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] St. Vincent's Hospital on the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] St. Vincent's Hospital for an operation and a little candy striper working there discovered his name on the chart and went home and told her folks "that somebody in the hospital with a last name of Hindes, could this be that long lost cousin?"

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Excuse me. Let me go back a little bit. She interviewed me. She was the receptionist and when she had taken all my history as they was taking it so it went on into the hospital records, she says "What was your mother's maiden name?" I said Mary Wood. She said "What was the middle name? And I said Mary Crossman Wood. And she looked me the funniest, you know, and went ahead and finished filling all of it out and put me up into bed and she took off for home as soon as her work was done and told her dad and mother that she'd run on to me. And here all of them was peeking through the door at me up in as I was laying in that room. I'd just been operated on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they Crossmans or Woods?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: They were Wood's. Yeah and so that's the way they found Chuck and I and for years we didn't even know where our mother was buried. Well, we knew where she was buried but we've never been to her grave and I guess Chuck never has been yet. Have, ya?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No, not yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, then your stepmother [Goldie Hindes] though, was who raised you.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: 'The flu epidemic began in 1917 and is commonly known as the Flu Epidemic of 1918 (see Neil Vanderburg, Monograph #8 and Velma Carter Rawie, Monograph #10). Charles and Norman's mother, Mary Crossman Wood Hindes, died of influenza in January 1919.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: This map [facing page] is referenced during interview and used on-site during tour. We have noted the existence of the store but no mention has been made of the approximate number of people, men, women and children possibly 75 or a few more living in camp. Grandma Mattney (Douglas Gilliam's maternal grandma), maintained a cook house for several single men that lived in the sizable bunk house. A large horse barn accommodating as many as six teams it seems was an impressive structure. Two large "Nash Quads" designed to run on large wooden rails flanged wheels kept the vehicle "on track." Neither vehicle was made operational prior to the 1929 shutdown. - C. H.

As I think back through those years, I think one of the reasons that they had to move us out. . . We were rambunctious kids and, in fact, little hellions. There's no doubt about that. We were kids that lived outdoors most of the time and we were around adults quite a bit of the time, so I think we were a little more mature and a little more prone to get into trouble than a lot of the kids. But, as I think back on those years, I think, bless her heart, that Mrs. Montgomery was going through a change of life. I've observed other women down through the years and I think that part of the problem was hers, as well as ours. But, anyway, the next year after we had completed at least one year at Tampico and possibly two, they got a small house that they made into a school house short of Elmer Govier's place, and hired Mrs. Blake as our teacher. She really turned the corner with us. She was an older, more mature woman and very well versed and had a knack of creating interest. entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Peeling poles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that in the Soap Creek area or the Tillamook area?

entries.speaker: A

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that's a new crop. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] They had two rollways there. They had a lower rollway and a upper rollway and they'd roll them logs on the trucks, with peavies .. .

entries.text: How long would a pole be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Hundred and twenties. There was some good piling up there.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 7. The Vandersantens' Hired Hands

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So, the Vandersantens. .. Were they doing their own logging or were they just selling the...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were in the cattle business.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] They didn't have anything to do with the lumber. They didn't have anything to do with the piling either. I think they owned the timber, didn't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] It could be. I'm sure about that. I kind of think they did, but they were immigrants from Arizona or New Mexico. Very interesting people. But primarily they were livestock people and they apparently had a fairly sizable operation down in either Arizona or New Mexico and they brought with them a very interesting character that was Mexican and apparently he killed somebody down in that area. He was still a wanted man and he used to wear two. 38's one on each hip.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this is even in 1928. You're watching a Mexican guy walk down Soap Creek with 38's on his hips.

chapters.title: Albert Zundt, The Rohners, and Agnes Dobrinin

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. Doing all of his farm work. Everything was done in, with guns in place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gosh. I don't. He and a fellow that was a veteran of World War I lived in Airlie and primarily commuted back and forth [His name slips my mind - CH].

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] It was Walter, something. We'll think of it shortly, but they used to drive back and forth and they were primarily livestock people. The Mexican more so than Walt. One time there was a dead cow to be buried. They had a span of mules on the place that they did a lot of their necessary farm work with. The Vandersantens sent my brother and I and the Mexican out with the team of mules and sled to pick up this animal and haul it off and bury it. The Mexican didn't want to do any more work than he had to, so he stood on the back of the sled, reigns in hand. The mules were kind of skittish anyway under certain circumstances, particularly with a dead animal around, and so he finally got the mules around to where they hadn't observed the dead animal yet, but they were close enough that we could start to roll the dead animal abroad. The Mexican standing on the back end holding the line was taut, and all of a sudden, the mules either smelled or saw this dead animal, and they just laid their ears back and they said, eeeahh, and took off. There was a mound ahead of them maybe just 18 inches high, but just enough to act as a fulcrum as this sled went over and it pitched this Mexican in the air about 10 feet and he came down on head and shoulders and six guns out, very unceremoniously on the ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old a man was he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He probably was 35, 40 years old.

entries.text: 9. Lee Brown

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember Stambaugh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Chuck] I didn't. Did you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or Hardingrass? Any stories about any of the crops in that area or farming at night? Any of the farmers in that particular. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We really didn't know or have much association with the farmers, even though my grandfather had been quite an extensive farmer. We really kind of lost track of farming by the time we got up there. I knew a little about Lee Brown's extensive sheep operation.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now I'd to hear more about that. We're moving kind of closer to the school there. Lee Brown. Was he living there at the same time that the Hildebrands. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. The Hildebrands moved in after Lee left. I'm not sure just what transpired there. Lee was living there and he was running extensive sheep flocks. entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2

entries.text: Well people were saying that dozens of people had lived there at times, and that they had a Store, and other people scoffed. They said, "No, we never had that many families in there."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No, there was these that I can remember, and I know there was probably two or three more that I have forgotten, so there's two, four, six, eight, ten homes. I can see twelve families there that I know for sure were there [and there] were several more.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Ivan Slater, he was a kid. He went out and he was a side rod for Weyerhauser [Corporation] for years, several years.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Ivan Slater?
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Uhh huh.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he lived up there in the mill?
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: His dad did.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Did you know him by chance?
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, but I've worked with GP [Georgia-Pacific] a lot and I've heard the name Slater. So Breniman, who lives down where Barzees lived, he moved there after the war. Was pretty big [with GP] in the south, too, so he's lived there since '51, so that'd be, so Ivan Slater lived there too.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well he didn't live there. He went to school in Salem and then he'd come over and visit his dad. His dad and mother lived there. His dad horse logged for the mill. .
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And he was courting a gal that was kind of our big sister and we didn't like that character at all.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Ivan Slater?
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Ivan Slater.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] He later married this girl.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Ivan Slater's wife was the daughter of Fred Slater's second marriage. That was his step sister that he married.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And of course back in those years he was just a few years older than we were and he had a Model T Ford chassis that he made into a bus body, and that was the popular thing in those years, so he'd come up there and court this gal. When he took off in the evening he'd put that old Model T in lower axle gear and just spin gravel all over as he departed. So we watched him do that a few times and thought well we're gonna try to get even with that guy for stealing our girl. We could see he was making more progress all the time with her. One night he parked the bug and went in to court her we went up to the barn and got a big log chain, about 30 feet long and we tied it around the back axle of that bug and to an oak tree and so that time when he took off he left the back axle practically in place and the bug body went bouncing down the road. We kids were hard to find from there on.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he ever find out who did it?
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm sure he knew. I'm sure he knew.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're talking about the petrified oyster you found near the "Indian fort."
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Near what was termed to us as the old Indian fort, and this would be located as you stood at the bottom of this tram road and looked almost due west and just a little bit north theres an area up there that some people have referred to as a clear cut, but I remember that as a large open meadow that never did have trees on it and this is probably the highest point as you're looking off in a generally westerly direction [Forest Peak] from the bottom of the tram road.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So, we'll be able to look at that out at Soap Creek.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay and that's where you recall that oyster.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: A

entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On location somewhere near Adair Village.
entries.chapter_ref: A. The Old Mill Site and Ivan Slater

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B. The Blake Place

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Let's get back so we can look in the driveway but I think that house, of course, has replaced the old Blake house, but I think looking at the one walnut tree over there and this oak tree, that that house was almost exactly where the old Blake home was. It may have set back a little further from the road that we're currently standing on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So we're looking at the number 29173. We're on the old road going back on. This is where Blakes lived.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this road that we're on used to go right into Tampico. I see the sign that says "dead end" now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, Ed Blake gave some interviews, like you guys are doing, but he did them in the 1920's and at that time he said he could sit out on the family porch and watch them taking the Indians to the reservation, and so if he's located here instead of [Highway] 99 that tells us that he was going the old Tampico Road, rather than the 99 route. I had no idea that he lived in a different location when he was being interviewed.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well, wouldn't you say the front porch was out on this [East] side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I don't remember the house in particular. It seemed like the front porch was on the west side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you think the front porch was looking east. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It may have wrapped around the house. It may have been the back porch that I'm thinking about, too.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. It was a big back porch just like that. I got a picture of Mrs. Blake standing there, when I grew up, on the front porch at home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, theres another story in which the Blakes talked about two girls that rode up to their house in the 1870's or 1880's and they stuck their riding crops in the ground and both crops started growing. They're made out of black locust and whats interesting. . . I think we're seeing an old walnut, but are those black locust back there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I kind of think maybe they are.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so theres black locust at the newer homestead so all along we've been marking those black locust, but these are the black locusts. That must've been the story.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. This was the original homeplace. Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, then that would make the porch facing west and the back porch facing east.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it could've been the back porch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, sure. They could've come up to the back porch.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] The front porch was long clear across here as I remembered it and Ed used to sit out there and Mrs. Blake and they could look out there. . . Ed owned all of that down through there where the big building is now. He farmed that. Now I wouldn't argue the point, Chuck.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, we're not arguing.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Maybe you're night.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's clarify here. We're rewriting history here a little bit. We got the wrong trees marked for the riding crops story for one, and that story was in 1930.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: That's it right there. I remember her talking about that. She used to be proud of that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Those are the trees and I think that house is probably very close to the Original location. The original house may have sit back another 20 or 30 feet, but it's very close to the same location.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when the Blakes moved over to the other place there, there was already a house there wasn't there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. There was an old run down house as I remember. I don't think it had been occupied for years and I think, if I remember right, they had a man working for him by the name of Johnson, I believe, and I think they turned this farm over to him and they more or less went into retirement and completely refurbished this other house where they both lived when they died. Now, wait a minute. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. They lived there when Ed died. Oh my gosh. Come to think of it, I've got to kind of contradict myself. They finally moved to town because they were living in town when Ed died, and also when Mrs. Blake went to the nursing home, because I took her to Salem from that residence down there about Sixth and Harrison in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So from that second house there they went to Sixth and Harrison. Could their hired hand's name have been Johnson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Johnson. It was Johnson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember his first name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: George or. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Something like that, Chuck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Rohner was telling me that a guy named Johnson lived across from the Blakes, but he said he was a hired hand but you think it may have been George Johnson.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think so.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Could've been very well.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think he was a single man as near as I recall, and had worked for Blakes for years and years and years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is only the second time we've heard of this man. This Johnson, so, and this would be the location. Well that's great. They couldn't place it on a map or anything, but now we've got a point on the map and. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That's it. That's right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything when you came to visit the Blakes, here, now, and you said they farmed out the whole area. He was a retired sheriff by that point, wasn't he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, he was deputy.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] He was the deputy for Benton County.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And I think he sold insurance too, kind of on the side. I think he was one of these Grange Insurance or Farmers Insurance or something like that. He kind of did that out of his home. He was a man that was a little bit allergic to hard work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Blake was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very nice gentleman, but he and hard work didn't gel well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting. He did a lot of talking, a lot of the history for this area. He kept that alive, but when people talked about anybody doing anything they talked about his wife being a School teacher.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was the real doer. They belonged to the Grange and anything that was a social nature. I never held Ed Blake in very high esteem as far as hard work was concerned. Not that that's any particular criterion, but Ed and hard work didn't seem to gel well.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] _ He never even liked to carry the milk in from the old barn when he'd milk the cow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you guys were kids and you'd come here on the weekend and then he'd kind of have you do chores or Johnson would be working?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Not too much. We were pretty much under Mrs. Blake's jurisdiction and she was giving us a home that we hadn't had up to that point. I had living with my grandparents, but my brother and the rest of the family didn't have that nice a home setting.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We didn't have that environment.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And this was a real cultured environment that you came into, and she would talk a little bit about history and a little bit about life in general, and it was kind of a nurturing experience.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She sounded like a really a nice person.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fantastic person.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] She's the one that started us. .. If my dad would've let me, she wanted me to stay over, Chuck and I both. She'd take us. Just keep us when the folks went to the valley and put us through school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Charlie Olson's told me almost the same story about Mrs. Blake, but 30 years before then. About 1900 or 1905. She's real influential and got them interested in the school and. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think we were her family. They never had children and I think she more or less made us the kind of a pseudo family, if you will.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Nobody liked us two because we was mouthy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just Mrs. Blake, huh?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah. Mrs. Blake understood us.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We always got one week. .. Chuck would be with a weekend and then I'd be a weekend.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Everything I've heard about her is along the lines of history and teaching and being just a real nice, influential person.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: She'd sit all during the noon hour and peel apples and feed us kids. All of the kids in school were the benefactors.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] We had a lunch program before there ever was a lunch program at Soap Creek School.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A free lunch program. Well, can you think of anything else?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No, except I'm going to have to go for home before damn long. I don't want to stay too long in one spot.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C. Return to Mill Site

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, back to the mill site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] This plank road started from the Soap Creek Road and went pretty much over close to the hill there about where that line of willows is. I think there was a little creek at that time. I think pretty much flowed year around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, that was a question I got on that creek. In the survey notes its called Spring Creek and its got a name and Charlie Olson says he can remember when there was fish in that creek [Charlie Olson: Monograph #7, p:82] and there was a small waterfall in it that came in about the school somewhere and now that thing's almost dry year around.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Umm. Hmm. Right.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] I can remember that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I don't remember there ever being enough water for fish in it, but there could have been.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] I don't ever remember. When we cut those trees, I don't ever remember crossing the creek there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, you know that was kind of swampy in there where we cut the trees actually.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, he was talking 30 years before you guys, too, and so here it is another 60 years later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We were speaking about that Indian fortification [Cultural Resource Inventory, pp:54- 59] in this area that this man thought was clear cut. Its this area right through the oak tree there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That ain't the one. Is it, Chuck? Isn't this back over that knoll.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's. Okay. Theres one hump that comes up and then theres a long ridge and it comes up to that knob up there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I guess you're right. Actually I think its a little further north.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] It is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So we're standing slightly . . . Southwesterly of the school.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now that logged off area in the foreground and directly behind that there's an open meadow which existed even when we were here, and supposedly on top of that hill is where the Indian fortification was, and that's where I found the petrified oyster.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On top of that hill there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On top of the hill.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] In the indentation in there where the indians reportedly fought from.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, now that's an interesting point, there. I had a man take me there four years ago. Jim Hanish, and he said there's fortifications there and Indian pits. So we found three pits that were almost filled in and he found a three and a half inch obsidian bi-face there. We've just found two more large artifacts up there, and one other person told me that theres supposed to be an indian fort there between. . . There's a long ridgeline heading toward Coffin Butte between this knob, which is Forest Peak and the next knob, which is called Writsman's Hill or Steele Hill. So this... What did you hear about that indian fort? Did anybody. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Not very much and it was pretty well filled in then.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We just found it and it was an Indian fort as far as we were concerned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Some people called it a. . . said it was built out of logs and another person said it was dug into the ground.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Dug into the ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think the story we had was that it was dug into the ground, but it was almost filled in. There were just slight indentations in the ground when we were there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember who told you those [Soap Creek Burial Site] stories?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I suspect it might have been Mrs. Blake. That would be the only person that we had contact with that knew anything about real ancient history in this area and she was great on Indian lore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, there's a Story that in the Soap Creek Valley that it was an Indian burial ground and that early residents here would hear the Indians wailing as they marched in here and somewhere on the Soap Creek Flats they'd bury their dead. Have you heard anything like that?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Never heard.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I never heard that story.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Mrs. Blake tell you any stories about any Indians through this area at all?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No. Not to my knowledge.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] None that I can remember just off hand, other than possibly this fortification up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Mrs. Stambaugh collected mortars and pestles below here, along this side of Coffin Butte, but we've only had one reported site within the whole valley where there's any arrowheads found to any degree. Can you remember anybody talking about digging up mortars and pestles or digging up arrowheads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not in this area. I have up around the Dallas area, but not here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's very...

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D. The Old Sawmill Camp

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] I'm going to walk up there. You guys go ahead. I'm going to see if I can't find that water tank location.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] They've been doing some rotor tilling up around here where the garden is and we uncovered some heavy glass and heavy cookware. I thought it was probably old home brew bottles.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] [UNINTELLIGIBLE].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got this recorder back on but we're up from the Vandersanten. . . their house and we're about where you think the plank road came through.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yes. We are about seven, eight hundred feet off the Soap Creek Road now, heading almost due east.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We've got a. . . kind of a road type surface right there. We've got a couple trees here that would keep it from being aligned up directly with here. They look over sixty years old.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's amazing how some of these trees grow. Near where the mill site was, we looked at about a two and half foot ash stump, and I found the growth rings on that, and they just about corresponded to the time we left here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That's about 24 inches in diameter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's with the other mill sites on the school property. People have been there and think they're in a natural area rather than an old industrial site. So the old plank road came up through here. Was there anybody living between here and the road then?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Oh, yeah. This is all part of the living area out here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. I see. Okay. So. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] In fact, we're just about where the store was.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] In fact, I think you were right, Chuck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well theres the Thurston home first, which would be. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: . . . Close to the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, no. Its down right straight almost due west from this point down where that clump of trees is. Its probably well two-thirds of the distance between here and Soap Creek Road. That would be the Thurston home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the school would be near where the [Charles] King place is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. We decided on the way up that the Modrell home - school house was half way between the Elmer Govier and Griffin place on the opposite side of the road.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That school, we never had nothing to do with it, speaking of the present school house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. The store here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Oh, the store. It should be right in closer to where we are standing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] The store was right along side the plank road and probably just right in close to this vicinity here and then we'd go on up the plank road and notice most of the homes are on the left side, as we go up toward the mill. East.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That'd be right out through there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there'd be up against that little hill through there and right out up through that flat there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Fairly close to the road there because now once you get off the road in the winter time you were in trouble, so the homes were, well you know, certainly within walking distance, and for those few people who had cars, they probably planked off a little driveway that they could drive into.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was this country's side like through here at that time?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Just a good deal like it is here at present.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Pretty much the same as it is now. Maybe some of the oak trees in the bottom were larger than the current trees that we are looking at and they, as I recall, were a foot and a half to two feet in diameter and forty, fifty [feet] high.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Chuck, this isn't too damn far from the horse barn.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Not too far, I think they're up around the bend here a little bit further to the south.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An old brick here. No, that's not an old brick. That's a rock with sharp breaks.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] [UNINTELLIGIBLE].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any building there where the schoolhouse is now, that you can recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No. Nothing was there.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That's where I shot my brother, Chuck, in the ass with my beebee gun. My beebee gun wasn't working, I thought. So I told him to go down and bend over and he did and I shot him. It was working, Jesus Christ, I passed him on... He was right after me. Unhappy as hell.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Some water flowed down through here, Bob.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Okay, now we're looking at the Spring Creek bed [flood plane] so at least on a. . . this past winter. That's all fresh. Is that maybe machined out there though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: caption
entries.text: Soap Creek Schoolhouse. This schoolhouse was not yet built when Charles and Norman lived in the Logging Camp. It is believed to have been built in 1932, the year after Chuck and Norm received certificates from Tampico School (p:23).

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I think that's just washed, Bob. Theres been a pretty good flow of water down through here and I'm looking at these cattails down further down. It makes me think that maybe this creek is still, has a certain amount of water going underground. You see the fescue is still fairly green there yet, so it would indicate the water is not too far away even though the creek is dry.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] One of you guys want some breakfast [Disputes a cooking artifact he discovers along the creek].
bracketed_corrections: [Disputes a cooking artifact he discovers along the creek]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, heres an old creek bed right through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No. I think we'll find that this creek probably divides up there someplace close to where the mill was located.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now there's . . . where those blackberries are. Sometimes those blackberries are pretty good predictors of old buildings sites.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Could very well have been the horse barn there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right where those blackberries are?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] [UNINTELLIGIBLE] roses over there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, it could be, Norman. I know there was quite a bit of room next to the Thompson house here that was relatively flat before you got into the hill.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. It was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And the thing that I don't see is any ash trees. They, too, like water and more so than the oak. I didn't think they cut all the ash out. Now theres a few ash trees right there. I kind of think the creek may have been at the side of the Plank road. The Thompson home was right here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] I wouldn't be at all surprised, Chuck. Just look back in the trees a little bit to the hill there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, were all these homes built in 1927 or '28? So this is like an instant mill town here and then after about two or three years it just started falling apart.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: They started building it in '27 I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Probably. We were here in about '28 and after looking at that photo, I can see that there were several houses missing so probably by '36 they'd started tearing down the houses.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Oh. I bet they did. People come in here and got the material and used the lumber for something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Now these houses were of rudimentary construction. I mean, all the lumber came right out of the mill in rough form.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What they call mill run?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all rough cut and for the most part the houses were verticle board and bat siding. Single wall construction, boxcar roof, no insulation overhead or in the walls or flooring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you say a boxcar roof. Does that mean a literal. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] It was like a boxcar. Just exactly.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yes. Just like a boxcar. Convex roof.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but I mean that's the style rather than it wasn't actually taken from a boxcar.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. It was the style.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Oh, no. It wasn't a boxcar.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And you could throw a cat through the cracks almost anyplace. In the winter time it took scads of wood just to even keep the frost off the windows.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] They got the tar paper to cover the roof and some of the side walls.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, inside, if you remember, we had a kind of a heavy building paper about the consistency of 15 pound felt, if you're familiar with that, and it was kind of grayish in color and once in a while why there'd be some wallpaper show up, but very seldom. For the most part it was just that old gray paper.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still, that had to be a real step up from the tent.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes indeed. We thought that we were in the next echelon of society. Yes, indeed. But by today standards, you'd question keeping any prize livestock in that same facility.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E. The Old Mill Site

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] The location of track for the Nash Quad is here and that's right above the old mill site. The Nash Quad was a vehicle that ran on wood rails - never made operational.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, theres a brick and it looks like another drainage and a jar over here. Heres some broken glass through here. Heres a new whiskey bottle.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's after your time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Whats that, Norm?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] [UNINTELLIGIBLE].

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Where the what was? The burner? Could be. Yeah, that's a Johnny-come-lately addition.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Says Old Stag, but its not that old. That's pretty new here, too.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: That's a brick, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Even the brick is new.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah. Another brick...

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, heres somebody's got some plants. Some iris or something and here we got some old metal. Ooo. Really old. It just broke in my hand.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I think that's part of the step for a buggy, Bob. It looks like it. Doesn't it to you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: It right out of here. I don't know what else we've got here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: _ And we got some linoleum. New stuff. It looks to me like we're definitely in an archeological site here. Can you see this through here? This looks like an old buggy wheel.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah, or Model A Ford. Model T Ford, maybe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they that narrow?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Mmm. Hmm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That must've been a sold rubber tire.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Was it? Was that narrow? Yeah, you're right. Yep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Might be a bicycle?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Bicycle. Yeah, I think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it would be early 1900's probably, huh?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Let's see. Theres where the spokes went.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, we've got a real mix of it looks like about 1920 to 1992 material here.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I'll tell you for sure, that we couldn't afford a bicycle. Now that's a regular kiln brick, so. Are you subject to poison oak?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. I really am and I get real bad but its one of the hazards of the trade.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Well, it doesn't bother me so I will lead the way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An old stove part. Oh, we've got a dump over here where Norman's at. Is that a new dump or an old dump, Norman?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Pretty old. It could be awful close to where that slab pile used to burn. I know the old camp used to throw all their old garbage and stuff in the slab pile.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It looks like somebodys been going through this garbage a little bit. Kind of segregating it but it looks like the same thing. A mix of old and new.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yeah. It very well could be, Bob.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Of course the newer times people could've just thrown away the older stuff but some of that we're finding back there is buried in the ground so its been there for a while.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Well, Chuck, where was it we figured the mill? Right in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yeah. Right up through there . . right in front of you.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well, it could be. . . See, that slab pile was about 150 feet from the mill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got a bunch of old boards through here, which would be. . . depending on how long they 've been out in the weather.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I don't figure out why the hell it wasn't just an old log, though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I started to dig it out but it started to crumble so I thought I'd just leave it. This man may be a collector may be an antique piece. . . Theres some more of them over there. . . That's a candlestick. . .

chapters.title: Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History
chapters.label: F.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That looks an old Cherokee stove, isn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Either that or a lamp.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, look at this right through here that's been gone through a whole lot. Theres bottles and rusted cans and pop tops and. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] I just wonder, if a guy had a shovel, you know as deep down here as we are one could find the old slab pile or burner site.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Oh, yeah but this guy probably would not appreciate our digging. His wife is probably an antique freak. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Oh, yeah. I imagine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Theres apt to be some really valuable bottles through here just from the looks of things but now theres been a lot of fire through here too and a lot of metal. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think that's what Norman was saying that this was a slab pile where they burned all the slab and sawdust and people threw their garbage in here as well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Huh, so that's how people got rid of their garbage. They just kind of hauled it over to the slab pile, huh? Well that would. . . Certainly theres a lot of evidence that shows that that's probably the case.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] See this was all houses up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, the houses were here, the slab pile was here. Wheres the mill from here, then?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, just right next door.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Right back up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think between your map and that aerial we could locate the thing, just about. Now, they've got an excavation over there and they've got a bunch of clearing going on up there. Those would be. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: That's where he's going to put his home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] That green grass indicates the water is not too far away. Now, the mill was located right in this area,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there a chance, where he's clearing up there, that he's moving up. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very likely. He said he uncovered some crockery up here. I thought I'd look. See, that's where our home was right in that enclosure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where his garden is.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. Only slightly above.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so that was the end of the line for the school district.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. The end of the line for the habitation of camp.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That doesn't look like burnt soil. Doesn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No, that looks like animal blood perhaps deer.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's one thing we haven't covered yet, and maybe we can do that next time is hunting and fishing.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, fishing was fairly good. Hunting was excellent. There were deer all over the place.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, where the Rohners were and Glenders at the other end of the valley there, with all those farms and stuff, they never saw deer. They say they'd see a deer every two or three
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: years but where Olson lived, which is up over in there a little bit, he said they fed the deer there were so many of them.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mmm. Hmm. Right.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you ever remember elk?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I never did see any elk here.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bear?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw any bear. They probably were here but I never saw them because that one photo you had shown some bear that were killed in the area.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep. So, now we're at your old home here, huh?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Heres a metal strap.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think that's probably from a cultivator. Now, those old stumps were probably what determines our outer boundary.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing I talked to people who are out through here and I keep asking what it looks like and they all say just about the same as now. That is was basically sixty and seventy year old trees that they'd cut out and now there are sixty and seventy year old trees up there again and it looks about the same. Was this all clear cut back up through here?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It was pretty much like it is now, Bob. Pretty much scrub growth and small timber.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We used to play in there.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] .. . to my knowledge this area, I don't think was ever logged at least I never recall finding any old stumps prior to our logging. All logging stops straight over in this area just south of us.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, lets see. I think this would be west through here.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, pretty much. I think west is right here.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, south or southwest.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Southwest. Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So, the logging area was up through there and then the horses would skid down to the mill into there. Did they have a mill pond?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It was all gravel. The skid road just kind of went right around the hill and gradually up. Started picking up steeper grade back in there and got to the point that it was steep enough that the horses would have to pull off the side and pull the dog out and let the logs shoot down over and then pick then up down below.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] A truck hauled the logs down off there past the water tank to the mill.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we're seeing a lot of bigleaf maple or maybe ash, but I think its bigleaf up there on the hill that's turning yellow. Was that hardwood up through there? Can you recall?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] No. That was all Douglas fir.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any sign of older trees in there, other than the trees you're logging. Any old stumps or snags or big old trees?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I recall seeing.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No old growth that I remember seeing.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This area here was all prairie in 1850. Pretty much everywhere through here, but there were a couple of patches of big trees. Do you recall seeing any around here at all?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Not that I remember, but it doesn't mean that they weren't here, but we saw some pretty good sized trees up around the Sulphur Springs area, but not right in here.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We never saw any big stuff till we got to Tillamook, and we got there before the burn.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the products that the other mills around here were cutting were ties. Railroad ties.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] A lot of output was tie material.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you said you were doing poles and piling individually and then for this mill here, what were they cutting?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just long saw timber, and this went out to what they call Wellsdale, right in the middle of where Camp Adair is now, and they had a planer mill up there and so they planed and shipped out on the railroad.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you call it Wellsdale or Wells?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wellsdale.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Did you ever hear it called Wells or Wells Station?
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wells Station. Yeah.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah, Wells Station.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Its another one of those places that's name kept changing through time.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yes. I remember when they first went from a four cylinder Chevrolet truck motor to the six cylinder. We thought that was a real powerhouse for hauling lumber out of here, believe it or not. We just stood back in awe when that thing belched and pulled out a load a lumber.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What year was that about? That'd have to be some of the first six cylinder GMC motors.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably '28.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because on the Berry Creek side, about 1930 or '31, we're getting the first cat logging and first log trucks, so it was a little bit earlier.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That was the year there wasn't a hell of lot doing. It was depression. When they got started again, about just after Roosevelt went in there with the NRA [National Recovery Act], in that area in there. Then they started getting these RD-7 and RD-6's and RD-4's.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I first learned to run cat in the CC's [Edward Sekermestrovich: Monograph #4] and that was late 1934. It was a Caterpillar #60 rear mounted bulldozer. The operator had to look over his shoulder all the time when building road.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that had to be some of the first dozer work done anywhere. That's about what year we're getting over in Berry Creek, too.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was 34 and '35. We built the road into Dean's Mountain, which is a primary fire lookout in the Elliot State Forest in SW Oregon near Reedsport. About 30 miles of road was built through virgin timber.
entries.chapter_ref: F. Hindes' Home Site and Local Logging History
