entries.text: G. Fishing and Trapping Stories

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At the store down here. . . What did they sell in that store?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty much all staples for household and to a degree, if women wanted lace or yardage material they'd bring it over from the store in Kings Valley because that was a very complete store.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Kings Valley store.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The big one. Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that was like a general mercantile or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. They had everything. Sold horse harnesses and collars and everything over at that store.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Everything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And so whatever this store needed over and above the grocery line, and very few vegetable products came from Kings Valley store.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would you go fishing around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever get down as far as the Glender's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think we fished that far. You didn't have to go that far. .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No. We didn't need to. Hell, we'd get 'em close to home.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] We'd get 'em here, you know, within a couple of mile stretch of camp.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember what kind of trout they were?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Brook trout.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think they probably were pretty much rainbow and maybe brook trout. Maybe even some brown's mixed in, but now species didn't mean anything to us then.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Anything edible.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What Gene [Eugene Glender] says that about 1934 or '35 they started getting rainbows in here. Before that they call them brook trout but they were... He thought they were probably cutthroat [Eugene Glender: Monograph #9].

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Could be.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well, they could have been. Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that the local name for the cutthroat was brook trout.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] That could very well be.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. That very easily could be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the biggest one you ever caught out of there?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Oh, about 14, 15 inches. A lot of that stuff was 14, 15. Hell, we'd come home with four or five a piece. We only used a string. We never used real fishing tackle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I asked three or four different people how big the fish got in the creeks here and 14 inches is what everybody says.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Is that right?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. So...

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well, twelve would be a good average.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So fishermen are supposed to exaggerate, but you're all the exaggerating the exact same number.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think one of the things that we did that probably upset the natives and our folks equally well was we'd ran trap lines, too, up and down the creek. In the fall we found a den of skunks in a hollow log, so we got forked sticks and ran in there and twisted and twisted until we'd get around the tail and then haul them back out and so we got, I think, four kits and maybe a female. And of course they saturated us good, and we threw those skunks over our back and walked right up that plank road and we had all the women in camp hollering at us and our folks made us take our clothes off and sleep outside.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Dad met us down the bottom of the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He could probably smell you from the bottom of the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] We had to take our clothes off and I'm not sure we didn't have to sleep outside for awhile.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever catch any beaver or see any beaver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not any beaver. Lots of mink.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Nope. No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Lots of mink in this country?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: Yes. Oh, there was lots of mink.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, now see by the '30's the mink were pretty gone.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I imagine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But, do you ever recall any stories of wolves?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No. We never heard anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: At the Vincent place there... That's where Charlie Olson claims he heard the last one was killed about 1905, something like that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Could've very well have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there anything other than mink?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Mink and skunk and muskrat.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Muskrat, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of wolverines in this country?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bobcats?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: No. Oh, well yeah there was cats around here but we never saw 'em.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about cougars? Did you ever hear. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Yes. I think there were cougars. You heard 'em but you never saw 'em.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: H. The Seabrook's Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the. . . Were there orchards around through this area where abandoned orchards or old orchards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the Vandersanten place there were trees particularly where this old house sat at the end of the road and where that barn is up there. There was some orchards up there, and I think there were a few trees around the Vandersanten house too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, the old place there. . .

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Well boys, I've got a hell a long ways yet to go tonight.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Theres an old piece of pipe or something. I don't know what its from.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] That where the nails had to be, Chuck. I wouldn't doubt it a bit if we are right in the slab pile location.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is only the second time you've been up here since you moved out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] That's right.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. Well, we was just more or less always afraid because of the sign down there. No trespassing and the other guy that owned it, we never did meet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're getting some stuff right here. Heres some glass, crockery. Heres some green glass. Heres a nail. We're on somebodys building site, right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think this was the Seabrook's place.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. Could've been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Heres some more metal right here. Do you know what happened to the families that were living here? Did they all move into here from Kings Valley with you guys?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: We don't know.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I don't know where they came from, Bob.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] We pulled out with that old Model T, we never looked back.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] Well, I'm not sure. It was almost like the immaculate conception the way they were just here and everybody moved in and I'm not just sure where people came from or went too.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Or where they went to after we left, either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is almost like an isolated community. That's why its been so hard to find out anything. Until you guys came along, because nobody knew anybody that was up here. They'd remember a name or two, and then nobody knows where they went. And you were just here just a short time, too, I think is a part of it.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: I can't figure where. . . Well, a lot of them, I think probably went back over around Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] That very well may be. I know the horse loggers left here for Kings Valley. Charlie Houris and Bobby Wallace were two that remember leaving.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Bobby Wallace. That was the other name I was looking for. That was the other horse logger?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Yeah. He had several teams here and then Slater, Old Fred Slater, he had one team.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was Fred Slater? Was he also from Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] I think he was from Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Originally he sent his kid to school in Salem. I think he was right around the Salem area, and I think that's where he returned to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, this guy's [Charles King] got a whole community to clean up before he builds. Are these generally pretty happy years of your life here, or just getting by and not paying much attention to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] We didn't know what was going on in the outside world.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] Oh, we was kids. Hell, we could eat damned old oak nuts and hazel nuts.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] And venison. Don't forget that.

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [NORMAN] And venison, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever find any old antlers in the woods? Like curly cue sheep or elk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [CHUCK] In fact, I don't remember ever finding any deer antlers in woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that right? Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know they had to be there. Both deer and elk, most particularly in up in the forest where we logged, but I never run on to any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Heres some more brick down through here, now. I've been hitting some chunks and pieces So this would be below the. . . No this would be about coming into the store here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right. The store was over by the north side of the tram road approximately 800' due east of the Soap Creek Road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old is the man that owns this place here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I'd say he's in his 50's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I. The Modrell Schoolhouse

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we agree on the location of the Modrell school house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I saw you stopping when I was talking with Norman. Theres a little area that's not plowed underneath that oak tree and theres that little ravine next to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's right where Charlie Olson showed me that he stayed with Mrs. Blake" in about 1903.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay, and theres a patch of weeds and thistles around there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right where the house stood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's just what he told me, too, so we got confirmation 90 years later, so that's gotta be pretty near it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I wonder why they're not plowing that. I'm going to have to find out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Well, I better run him [Norman] back, Bob because he is getting impatient.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: END OF TAPE

entries.text: "When conditions warranted, both schools would operate simultaneously, as occurred between 1924 and 1941." - If memory serves me correctly we walked from the logging camp we visited with you to the "Tampico" school (jct: Tampico Rd and Soap Creek Rd.) for the 1927 school year. In the 1928 school year Alvie Govier converted a Model T truck into a school bus and transported the farm and mill kids to "Tampico with Mrs. Montgomery as teacher. For the 1929 and post of 1930 years Mrs. Ed Blake was brought to the old "Modrell" home converted to a school house - house located west side of "Soap Creek Rd" approximately half way between the Griffin and Elmer Govier farms.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Page 27* - Two tramroads (planked road ways with metal rails) connected the camp to the rest of the Soap Creek community. During my time at the camp (1927-30 and for a short stay in 1935) the only rails worked have been wooden. There was a short section of wooden rails laid for two "Nash Quads" that were designed to transport logs from the woods to the mills. The program was a complete failure - the machines were off the tracks so such of the time the project was abandon in favor of a skid road and horses.

entries.text: And about those three boys in the Hindes family, stepbrother, Douglas Gilliam, Norman and Charles Hindes, two are in their early 80's now and the third one will be 78 this year, 1996. All three have spent the majority of their productive years in the timber industry. All three are veterans of W.W.II. In retirement all three continue to reside in their birth state, Oregon, not far from Soap Creek. -- Charles Hindes, March, 1996.
